text: I would like to express my enormous concerns over this administration's executive order that will alter how grant funding is handled by the US government. Under the system that had made the US a scientific superpower, peer reviewers rated the scientific quality and feasibility of grant applications, and subject-matter experts within the funding agencies used these ratings to determine which grants got funded. Under the proposed rules, political appointees would have the final say, and they were specifically instructed not to “routinely defer” to peer reviewers. Overriding this process undercuts the credibility and viability of the US scientific community and its international status, and is not in the national interest. Allowing political appointees who have not been vetted for their scientific credentials to override and control the research grant vetting process is akin to giving an unlicensed or inexperienced physician and friend of the hospital CEO the power to make triage decisions in a high-volume emergency room. The US research community has always been the envy of the world, but no more, as it is being systematically dismantled and undermined for political objectives and ideologies. The consequences are both immediate, in terms of losing brain-power to other countries (already happening), and long-term because of the unintended or intended consequences of not funding research that is not "politically correct." Musser Street, Suite 100, Carson City, NV 89701 July 13th, 2026 The Honorable Russell T. Vought Director Office of Management and Budget 725 17th Street NW Washington, DC 20503 Re: State of Nevada Comments on Proposed Rule – Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance (OMB- 2026-0034) Dear Director Vought: The State of Nevada appreciates the opportunity to provide comments regarding the Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) proposed rule, Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance (OMB-2026-0034). These comments reflect the collective input of Nevada state agencies responsible for administering federal financial assistance across public safety, education, health and human services, transportation, environmental protection, broadband infrastructure, higher education, natural resources, libraries, Tribal affairs, and economic development. Collectively, these agencies manage hundreds of federal awards annually and administer federal resources through local governments, Tribal governments, school districts, institutions of higher education, nonprofit organizations, and other subrecipients responsible for delivering essential public services to Nevadans. Nevada appreciates OMB's continued efforts to modernize the Uniform Guidance and shares the Administration's commitment to strengthening accountability, improving stewardship of federal funds, reducing fraud, and promoting effective program management. Nevada has made significant investments in enterprise grants management, statewide training, risk assessment, internal controls, and modernization initiatives designed to improve accountability while supporting efficient administration of federal financial assistance. While Nevada supports many of the objectives outlined in the proposed rule, our agencies identified concerns with several proposed revisions that, if included in the final rule, may substantially increase administrative burdens and costs, create implementation uncertainty, reduce operational flexibility, and delay the delivery of federally funded services without proportionate improvements in program integrity. Many of the proposed revisions would require significant changes, within a limited amount of time, to agency policies, technology systems, staffing models, subrecipient oversight processes, and legal review functions. Of paramount concern is the effect on programs serving Nevada's rural communities, Tribal Nations, institutions of higher education, public safety agencies, healthcare providers, infrastructure investments, and local governments. The State respectfully offers the following comments from an operational and implementation perspective. Our recommendations are intended to support OMB's goals of transparency, accountability, and responsible stewardship while preserving the State’s ability to effectively administer complex federal programs and deliver critical and reliable services to the public. Nevada Governor’s Office of Federal Assistance | 2 I. Balancing Accountability with Administrative Efficiency State agencies administering federal financial assistance support OMB's efforts to strengthen accountability, improve stewardship of federal funds, reduce fraud, and promote consistent administration of federal financial assistance. Agencies agree that strong internal controls, sound financial management practices, and effective oversight are essential to maintaining public trust and ensuring federal investments achieve their intended outcomes. In reviewing the proposed rule, Nevada agencies have concerns that, when implemented collectively, the proposed revisions will substantially increase the administrative responsibilities of recipients and pass-through entities. The cumulative effect would require significant updates to policies and procedures, grant agreements, financial management systems, internal controls, procurement practices, and subrecipient oversight processes. Agencies also anticipate additional investments in staff training, legal review, technology enhancements, documentation, reporting, and compliance activities. With a limited implementation timeframe, these provisions risk affecting state budgets and reducing agencies’ ability to administer and deliver critical, reliable services to Nevadans. Nevada agencies currently administer federal awards within an established system of financial reporting, Single Audit requirements, risk assessments, internal controls, performance reporting, and ongoing federal oversight. The State is concerned that some proposed requirements may duplicate activities already required under current federal regulations, creating inefficiencies rather than enhancing existing oversight mechanisms. The administrative impacts of the rule, as proposed, would extend beyond state government. As federal grant recipients update agreements and compliance expectations, local governments, Tribal Nations, school districts, institutions of higher education, nonprofit organizations, and other subrecipients will face increased responsibilities. Rural communities may face disproportionate challenges because many have limited administrative capacity. Nevada supports continued modernization of the Uniform Guidance and OMB's objective of improving consistency and accountability across federal financial assistance programs. At the same time, modernization should remain practical, risk-based, and proportional to the complexity of the award so recipients can efficiently and reliably administer federal programs and deliver intended services. To that end, the State of Nevada respectfully recommends OMB: • Evaluate the cumulative administrative impact of the proposed revisions across the entire grant lifecycle. • Preserve risk-based compliance approaches that recognize differences in award size, complexity, and recipient capacity. • Avoid duplicative documentation and reporting requirements where existing federal oversight mechanisms already achieve the intended objective. • Continue balancing strong financial stewardship with efficient program administration and measurable program outcomes. • Provide time for successful implementation, clear implementation guidance, and technical assistance to promote consistent application across all federal awarding agencies. Nevada Governor’s Office of Federal Assistance | 3 II. Preserving Flexibility in State Administration of Federal Awards Nevada urges OMB to preserve the flexibility states need to administer federal financial assistance effectively. State agencies serve as direct recipients, pass-through entities, and oversight agencies, and they administer programs that vary significantly in size, complexity, statutory requirements, and delivery models. Maintaining flexibility within the Uniform Guidance allows states to tailor oversight based on program risk while continuing to meet federal accountability standards. As drafted, the proposed revisions expand recipient and pass-through entity responsibilities in ways that may reduce administrative flexibility without corresponding improvements in oversight. Proposed changes related to subrecipient monitoring, payment verification, national policy requirements, and additional compliance certifications may require more prescriptive administrative processes regardless of program size or risk. Nevada's existing risk-based monitoring practices have been effective in identifying compliance issues while directing oversight resources where they are needed most. Many Nevada agencies also administer federal funding through local governments, school districts, Tribal governments, institutions of higher education, nonprofit organizations, and other subrecipients. Several proposed provisions may require pass-through entities to assume additional monitoring and compliance responsibilities beyond administration of the federal award itself. Broad or undefined requirements could lead to inconsistent interpretations among federal awarding agencies and increase the compliance burden for both recipients and subrecipients. When finalizing the rule, the State urges OMB to provide clear definitions, consistent guidance, and reasonable implementation expectations to reduce uncertainty, help recipients understand their responsibilities, and promote uniform application across federal agencies. Nevada also encourages OMB to preserve existing state oversight processes where they already achieve accountability and fiscal stewardship objectives. Many agencies have established successful risk assessment procedures, financial controls, monitoring practices, and payment verification processes aligned with current Uniform Guidance requirements. Rather than replacing these processes with more prescriptive federal requirements, OMB should recognize existing state controls that effectively mitigate risk and ensure compliance. Infrastructure and pass-through programs also highlighted the importance of maintaining flexibility to administer awards using funding models that best support program delivery. Nevada agencies administering large infrastructure investments are concerned that eliminating established grant administration tools, including fixed-amount subawards for appropriate milestone-based projects, will significantly increase administrative workload and delay project implementation without improving accountability. Programs built around verified performance milestones incorporate extensive monitoring, reporting, and audit requirements that provide meaningful oversight while supporting efficient project delivery. It is the State’s position that effective grants management requires a balance between strong federal oversight and the flexibility to administer programs in a manner that reflects their statutory requirements, funding structures, and operational risks. Preserving this balance in the final rule will help states remain effective stewards of federal funds while ensuring administrative requirements support, rather than hinder, timely program and service delivery. Nevada Governor’s Office of Federal Assistance | 4 In a final rule, the State of Nevada respectfully recommends OMB: • Preserve risk-based oversight principles that allow recipients and pass-through entities to tailor monitoring activities based on program complexity and risk. • Issue timely guidance clarifying recipient and pass-through entity responsibilities for new national policy requirements before the rule is fully implemented. • Recognize existing state financial management, monitoring, and payment verification practices where they achieve the objectives of the Uniform Guidance. • Avoid unnecessarily shifting additional compliance responsibilities to pass-through entities without corresponding statutory authority or implementation guidance. • Preserve administrative flexibility for infrastructure and performance-based programs where existing oversight mechanisms have demonstrated effective accountability. III. Ensuring Predictability Throughout the Grant Lifecycle Effective administration of federal financial assistance depends on a predictable and stable regulatory environment throughout the grant lifecycle. State agencies make long-term commitments related to staffing, procurement, contracts, subrecipient agreements, technology investments, and program implementation based on the requirements in place when federal awards are accepted. Significant changes during the life of an award can create operational challenges, increase administrative costs, and delay federally funded services and projects. Nevada recognizes the importance of appropriate federal tools to address fraud, waste, abuse, and material noncompliance. However, broader discretionary suspension and termination authorities, if not clearly defined and consistently applied, would create uncertainty for state budgets and recipients administering multi-year programs and investments. Clear standards in a final rule will help recipients plan and manage federal awards while maintaining accountability and reliable program delivery. Reasonable implementation and transition periods are necessary when significant federal requirements change. Many state programs operate under multi-year awards or are already in advanced stages of planning and implementation. Applying new administrative requirements to programs designed under an existing framework may require recipients to revise award documents, update policies and procedures, renegotiate subrecipient agreements, and modify administrative processes. Without adequate transition time, these changes may compromise program effectiveness and delay federally funded services. Nevada agencies administering infrastructure and capital investment programs expressed particular concern regarding changes that could require established grant administration models to be substantially redesigned after project planning has already occurred. As one example, Nevada's Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) Program has completed extensive federal planning requirements, competitive provider selection, and pre-award activities under the current Uniform Guidance framework. Significant changes to award administration requirements at this stage would require the State to modify existing award structures and delay project implementation despite years of planning and coordination with federal partners. The State encourages OMB to maintain consistent federal guidance throughout award administration. Predictability allows state agencies to make informed decisions, establish reliable internal controls, and Nevada Governor’s Office of Federal Assistance | 5 implement programs with confidence that compliance expectations will remain stable over the life of the award. Where changes are necessary, OMB should provide sufficient guidance and transition time to minimize disruption. A predictable grants management framework benefits both federal awarding agencies and recipients by reducing administrative uncertainty, supporting long-term planning, and allowing agencies to focus on delivering federally funded programs efficiently and effectively. In a final rule, the State of Nevada respectfully recommends OMB: • Clearly define the circumstances under which suspension and termination authorities may be exercised and apply those standards consistently across federal awarding agencies. • Provide reasonable implementation and transition periods for significant regulatory changes affecting existing awards and programs already in implementation. • Recognize the reliance interests of recipients that have planned and administered programs under the current Uniform Guidance framework. • Minimize disruptions to ongoing infrastructure, capital improvement, and other long-term federal investments by allowing sufficient flexibility during implementation of new requirements. • Issue timely government-wide guidance to support consistent interpretation and application of the final rule throughout the grant lifecycle. IV. Ensuring Effective Implementation Across Federal Assistance Programs Nevada agencies administer federal financial assistance across programs that differ in statutory purpose, funding structure, operational requirements, and recipient capacity. Successful implementation of any regulatory changes will depend on recognizing these differences. As drafted, the State is concerned that the proposed revisions will affect rural communities, Tribal governments, institutions of higher education, local governments, nonprofit organizations, healthcare providers, public safety agencies, libraries, environmental programs, and infrastructure investments in different ways. Requirements that larger organizations can absorb may create unintended challenges for smaller entities with limited staffing and administrative capacity. Nevada therefore encourages OMB to account for differences in program scale, delivery model, and recipient capacity when finalizing and implementing the rule. Pass-through entities also play a central role in providing technical assistance, monitoring compliance, updating award documents, training subrecipients, and supporting consistent implementation across diverse recipient networks throughout the life of a federal award. Clear, timely, and consistent guidance from federal awarding agencies will be essential to successful implementation of a final rule. For infrastructure and capital investment programs, changes to long-standing grant administration practices could delay project delivery and increase administrative costs. Programs involving broadband deployment, environmental infrastructure, public works, and other long-term investments often require years of planning, procurement, engineering, environmental review, and coordination with local partners before construction begins. Requirements affecting award administration during implementation could disrupt and delay projects already underway. V. Recommendations and Conclusion The State of Nevada appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed revisions to the Uniform Guidance. Taken together, Nevada's comments emphasize that accountability, predictability, flexibility, and administrative efficiency can work together to strengthen federal financial assistance programs and support timely delivery of services to the communities federal funding is intended to benefit. text: See attached file(s) --- ATTACHMENT CONTENT --- 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 1 July 13, 2026 Office of Management and Budget Docket OMB-2026-0034 Re: RFI Response: Office of Management and Budget Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance Summary The University Corporation for Advanced Internet Development (d/b/a "Internet2") appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Office of Management and Budget’s proposed revisions to the Uniform Guidance governing Federal Financial Assistance. We support the federal government's efforts to strengthen accountability, improve stewardship of taxpayer resources, and ensure that federal research investments advance the nation's strategic priorities. As the operator of the nation’s leading research and education network and trusted digital infrastructure serving the U.S. research and education community, Internet2 offers a perspective centered on implementation. Our perspective is informed by our role as shared national research infrastructure rather than as a recipient of research funding alone. Today’s national research priorities increasingly depend upon shared cyberinfrastructure that enables secure collaboration among universities, federal agencies, national laboratories, industry partners, and regional research and education networks. National initiatives such as the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission, the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and future research infrastructure programs rely upon these shared capabilities to translate federal investments into scientific and economic impact. Internet2 respectfully encourages OMB to refine several aspects of the proposed rule to provide greater clarity, predictability, and consistency while preserving the collaborative foundations of the nation’s research enterprise. Our recommendations focus on strengthening implementation of federal research priorities by promoting clear policy guidance, objective compliance standards, predictable grants management, and sustained investment in the shared infrastructure that enables research at scale. We respectfully offer these recommendations from the perspective of an organization that works every day with federal agencies, research institutions, regional research and education networks, industry partners, and the private sector to strengthen the infrastructure that underpins American science and innovation. We believe these recommendations will improve implementation of federal research investments while preserving the collaborative ecosystem that has long supported U.S. scientific leadership, innovation, and economic competitiveness. About Internet2 Internet2 is a member-driven, nonprofit organization that provides advanced networking, cloud solutions, trust and identity services, cybersecurity capabilities, and other technology services that support the nation’s research and education enterprise. Our community includes more than 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 2 350 U.S. universities, 57 affiliates and federal affiliates, more than 60 corporations, over 40 regional research and education networks, and hundreds of research, education, healthcare, cultural, and nonprofit organizations. Internet2 convenes experts from industry, academia, and government to build community, share technical expertise, and collaborate to solve the nation’s technological and scientific challenges of both the present and future. For thirty years, Internet2 has operated the nation’s leading research and education network, providing the high-performance digital infrastructure that enables researchers to collaborate across institutions, disciplines, and geographic boundaries. Our network and services support research sponsored by virtually every major federal science agency, including the National Science Foundation, Department of Energy, National Institutes of Health, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, National Institute of Standards and Technology, Department of Defense, and other federal partners. Through the InCommon Federation and related trust and identity services, Internet2 also helps provide the secure, interoperable access that enables researchers, educators, students, and institutions to collaborate with confidence. Recommendation 1: Preserve Merit-Based Review While Providing Clear Alignment with National Priorities Internet2 supports the principle that federal research investments should advance the nation’s strategic priorities. Successive Administrations have appropriately identified emerging areas of national importance, including artificial intelligence, advanced computing, quantum information science, biotechnology, cybersecurity, and other fields that are critical to U.S. competitiveness, economic growth, and national security. Clear policy direction from federal leadership plays an important role in shaping these investments. The proposed rule’s provisions regarding agency head authority over award decisions reflect this principle. At the same time, the long-term strength of the federal research enterprise has been built upon transparent competition, independent scientific and technical merit review, and the confidence that funding decisions are guided by both national priorities and expert evaluation. These complementary principles have enabled the United States to pursue ambitious national objectives while maintaining the excellence and credibility of federally supported research. From Internet2’s perspective, this balance is particularly important because many of today’s national initiatives depend upon collaboration among universities, federal agencies, national laboratories, nonprofit organizations, regional research and education networks, and private sector partners. Shared infrastructure initiatives such as the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission and the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource rely upon trusted partnerships that are strengthened by transparent and predictable decision-making processes. Internet2 recommends that OMB clarify how agency leadership and expert merit review should work together within the proposed framework. Specifically, we recommend that the final rule: (1) affirm that merit-based peer review remains a core component of the award process even as agency heads exercise authority to align investments with national priorities; (2) require that agencies document the basis for award decisions, including how both merit review outcomes and strategic alignment were considered; and (3) provide guidance on how agencies should communicate priority shifts to applicants and existing 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 3 award recipients. These measures would preserve confidence in the integrity, transparency, and consistency of the federal research enterprise while supporting the Administration’s policy objectives. Recommendation 2: Establish Clear and Objective Standards for Compliance Internet2 supports efforts to improve accountability and consistency in the administration of federal financial assistance. Clear and objective compliance expectations benefit both federal agencies and award recipients by reducing uncertainty, improving efficiency, and allowing institutions to devote more resources to research and implementation rather than administrative interpretation. The proposed rule introduces references to “Gold Standard Science” as a compliance standard without establishing objective criteria for demonstrating compliance. As written, the term is not defined with reference to existing, widely accepted scientific standards or agency-specific review frameworks. Institutions and federal agencies may therefore interpret this requirement differently, resulting in inconsistent implementation across agencies and additional administrative burden for award recipients. This concern is particularly acute for organizations such as Internet2 that support research across multiple federal agencies, each of which may develop its own interpretation of “Gold Standard Science” in the absence of uniform criteria. As an organization that operates shared infrastructure serving hundreds of institutions and dozens of federal partners, Internet2 has consistently found that common standards, transparent guidance, and interoperable policies enable more efficient collaboration and reduce unnecessary complexity across the research ecosystem. To improve implementation, OMB should define “Gold Standard Science” using clear, objective, and measurable criteria that can be implemented consistently across federal agencies. OMB could accomplish this in several ways, including: (a) defining the term with reference to existing, widely accepted standards, such as National Academies frameworks, established agency peer review criteria, or other recognized scientific integrity standards; (b) delegating the development of agency-specific definitions through a structured process that ensures consistency across the federal government; or (c) replacing the term with reliance on existing compliance mechanisms already embedded in the Uniform Guidance and agency-specific regulations. Whichever approach OMB adopts, clear and uniform standards will strengthen accountability while providing institutions with the certainty needed to effectively administer federally funded research. Recommendation 3: Promote Predictability for Long-Term Research Infrastructure Investments Many of the nation’s highest-priority scientific initiatives rely upon infrastructure that is planned, built, and sustained over many years. High-performance research networks, trust and identity services, advanced cybersecurity capabilities, cloud connectivity, data platforms, and regional 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 4 research and education networks require stable investment and long-term operational planning to support the research community effectively. Internet2 has seen this firsthand through its engagement with initiatives such as the Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission and the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource. These efforts depend not only on individual research awards, but also on shared infrastructure that enables researchers from institutions across the country to securely access computing resources, exchange data, collaborate across organizational boundaries, and participate in national-scale scientific initiatives. These capabilities support thousands of researchers simultaneously and cannot be developed or sustained through short-term planning horizons. Greater predictability in the administration of federal awards also strengthens the ability of universities, nonprofit organizations, regional research and education networks, and other infrastructure providers to recruit and retain highly skilled technical staff, make responsible capital investments, and build durable partnerships that advance federal priorities over time. As Internet2 has observed through its workforce development partnerships, stable career-track positions for research computing and cyberinfrastructure professionals depend upon reliable funding horizons. While agencies should retain appropriate flexibility to respond to changing circumstances, organizations responsible for shared national infrastructure benefit from greater clarity regarding how and when active awards may be modified or terminated. Internet2 recommends that OMB provide additional guidance regarding the circumstances under which active awards may be modified or terminated due to changing agency priorities. Specifically, we recommend that the final rule: (1) establish minimum notice periods before agencies may modify or terminate active awards for reasons other than cause, providing award recipients with reasonable time to adjust operations; (2) define the categories of circumstances that may justify mid-award modifications, such as changes in statutory authority, appropriations, or national security requirements; and (3) require agencies to consider the impact on shared infrastructure and multi-institutional collaborations when making modification or termination decisions. Greater predictability will strengthen long-term planning, reduce unnecessary risk, and enable continued investment in the shared infrastructure that supports federally funded science. Recommendation 4: Preserve the Collaborative Infrastructure of American Science Scientific discovery depends not only on research funding, but also on the ability of researchers to exchange ideas, share results, build professional networks, and develop collaborative partnerships. Conferences, peer-reviewed publications, professional societies, and community- driven technical forums provide the foundation through which federally funded research is disseminated, evaluated, and translated into future scientific advances. Internet2 regularly convenes universities, federal agencies, regional research and education networks, scientific societies, technology companies, and nonprofit organizations to accelerate adoption of emerging technologies and strengthen collaboration around national priorities. Our community has supported convenings related to advanced networking, cybersecurity, trust and 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 5 identity, artificial intelligence, and other strategic initiatives, including hosting the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR) Annual Meeting in partnership with the National Science Foundation. These activities demonstrate that collaboration is not ancillary to research. It is an essential component of how research ecosystems function and how federal investments achieve lasting impact. Reasonable participation in conferences, publication of research results, engagement with professional societies, and other collaborative activities should continue to be recognized as legitimate and necessary components of federally supported research. To the extent the proposed rule introduces new restrictions or prior approval requirements for conference attendance, travel, or publication costs, Internet2 respectfully urges OMB to consider the practical consequences for research dissemination and collaboration. Specifically, Internet2 recommends that OMB preserve the long-standing framework under which reasonable conference participation, publication costs, and professional engagement remain allowable expenditures when they directly support federally funded research. Specifically, we recommend that the final rule: (1) maintain conference attendance and travel as allowable costs without requiring prior approval, provided that participation is directly related to the funded research; (2) preserve publication costs, including open-access publication fees, as allowable direct costs; and (3) establish clear safe harbors for participation in professional society activities and community-driven technical forums that advance federally funded research objectives. These measures will strengthen collaboration across the national research enterprise while maintaining appropriate stewardship of federal funds. Recommendation 5: Support Secure and Trusted International Scientific Collaboration Internet2 recognizes the importance of protecting U.S. research from inappropriate foreign influence and supports efforts to strengthen research security, safeguard sensitive technologies, and ensure compliance with applicable laws and national security requirements. At the same time, many of today’s scientific challenges are inherently international. Advances in areas such as climate science, astronomy, high-energy physics, genomics, public health, and advanced computing increasingly depend upon collaboration among trusted research institutions around the world. Secure international partnerships have long contributed to U.S. scientific leadership and remain an important component of the nation’s research enterprise. Internet2’s network connects the U.S. research and education community with trusted research and education networks across the globe, enabling secure collaboration among universities, national laboratories, scientific facilities, and research organizations. Through trusted networking, federated identity, and established security practices, Internet2 helps provide the infrastructure that enables international collaboration while supporting responsible stewardship of research data and resources. Internet2 recommends that OMB ensure any restrictions on international collaboration remain appropriately tailored to legitimate national security risks while preserving trusted 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 6 scientific partnerships that strengthen U.S. research leadership, competitiveness, and innovation. Specifically, we recommend that the final rule: (1) adopt a risk-based, tiered approach that distinguishes between fundamental research, which benefits from openness, and sensitive applied research, which may require controls; (2) rely upon existing research security frameworks, such as those established under NSPM-33 and agency-specific foreign influence disclosure requirements, rather than introducing duplicative obligations; and (3) provide clear guidance on how award recipients should evaluate international collaborations, including safe harbors for engagement with allied nations’ research institutions through established trust frameworks such as international research and education networking agreements. Recommendation 6: Recognize Shared National Research Infrastructure as a Strategic Asset and Leverage Existing Collaborative Capabilities Federal research investments increasingly depend upon shared national research infrastructure that extends well beyond individual grant recipients. High-performance research networks, trust and identity services, secure cloud connectivity, advanced cybersecurity capabilities, regional research and education networks, and collaborative digital platforms enable researchers from institutions of every size to participate in federally funded science. These capabilities have become foundational components of the nation's research enterprise and should be recognized alongside traditional research investments as strategic infrastructure supporting U.S. scientific leadership. This shared infrastructure enables researchers to securely access advanced computing resources, move and analyze large scientific datasets, collaborate across institutional boundaries, and connect to national laboratories, scientific user facilities, cloud providers, and specialized research instruments. It also expands access to federally funded research by allowing smaller and emerging research institutions to participate in national scientific initiatives through shared capabilities they could not reasonably develop on their own. The complexity of today’s scientific challenges also requires collaborative implementation models that leverage the complementary strengths of federal agencies, universities, nonprofit organizations, regional research and education networks, national laboratories, cloud providers, and private sector partners. Organizations such as Internet2 and the regional research and education networks represented by The Quilt provide enduring operational capabilities that enable federal agencies to rapidly engage broad segments of the research community without duplicating existing infrastructure or creating new organizational structures. Building upon these established partnerships improves efficiency, expands participation, accelerates implementation, and maximizes the return on federal research investments. Policies that introduce uncertainty into long-term planning or impose administrative requirements that are not well suited to shared infrastructure organizations may unintentionally weaken the collaborative ecosystem upon which thousands of federally funded research projects depend. Conversely, predictable grants management policies encourage long-term investment, 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 7 strengthen institutional partnerships, and enhance the federal government’s ability to rapidly implement emerging national priorities. Internet2 respectfully recommends that OMB explicitly recognize the essential role of shared national research infrastructure when finalizing this rule, and preserve flexibility for federal agencies to leverage existing collaborative capabilities in implementing national research priorities. Specifically, we recommend that the final rule: 1. Recognize shared national research infrastructure, including advanced networking, trust and identity services, cybersecurity capabilities, and collaborative cyberinfrastructure, as essential components of the federal research enterprise. 2. Ensure that grants management policies support, rather than inadvertently disrupt, long-term operational partnerships and shared infrastructure that enable research communities across multiple institutions and sectors. 3. Preserve flexibility for agencies to use collaborative implementation models that leverage existing nonprofit organizations, regional research and education networks, and public-private partnerships to advance national research priorities. These refinements will strengthen the federal government’s ability to translate research investments into scientific discovery, technological innovation, workforce development, and long-term national competitiveness. Conclusion Internet2 appreciates OMB’s thoughtful consideration of these comments and shares the goal of ensuring that federal research investments advance the nation’s strategic priorities while delivering meaningful scientific, economic, and societal benefits. As OMB finalizes this rule, we respectfully encourage particular attention to four areas that will strengthen implementation of federal research investments: • establishing clear and objective compliance standards; • providing greater predictability for long-term research infrastructure investments; • recognizing shared national research infrastructure as an essential component of the federal research enterprise; and • preserving the collaborative ecosystem that enables federally funded science to thrive. Internet2 stands ready to continue working with OMB, federal agencies, and partners across the research and education community to strengthen the nation’s research infrastructure and support implementation of future national priorities. 1150 18th Street NW Suite 750 Washington, DC 20036 phone 202.803.8995 8 Respectfully submitted, ------ /s/Belinda Nixon Belinda Nixon Vice President and General Counsel Internet2 bnixon@internet2.edu

text: Please see attached comments. --- ATTACHMENT CONTENT --- July 13, 2026 Andrew Reisig / Joel Savary Office of Management and Budget Office of Federal Financial Management 725 17th Street, NW Washington, DC 20503 RE: Docket Number: OMB-2026-0034 Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance The Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance (CVSA) respectfully submits the following comments in response to the proposed rule published in the Federal Register by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) on May 29, 2026. Specifically, OMB is seeking comments on the agency’s proposal to revise the Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance, located in Title 2 of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), Subtitle A, to improve government-wide policies and requirements related to the management of grants, cooperative agreements and other forms of assistance, Docket No. OMB-2026-0034. About CVSA CVSA is a nonprofit association comprised of local, state, provincial, territorial and federal commercial motor vehicle safety officials and industry representatives. The Alliance aims to achieve uniformity, compatibility and reciprocity of commercial motor vehicle inspections and enforcement by certified inspectors dedicated to driver and vehicle safety. Our mission is to improve commercial motor vehicle safety and uniformity throughout Canada, Mexico and the United States, by providing guidance and education to enforcement, industry and policy makers. CVSA has four membership types: • Class I Members – Our state/provincial/territorial agencies are represented by various police agencies/departments, highway patrols, departments of transportation, public utility and service commissions, departments of motor vehicles, and ministries of transportation. • Class II Local Members – Our local agencies are represented by city or municipal police departments. • Class III Associate Members – Our associate members are companies, organizations, trade associations, trucking and bus companies, industry suppliers and vendors, training institutions, consultants, insurance companies, state or provincial trucking associations, and large- and small-fleet owners, and owner operators. • Class IV Federal Members – Our Class IV members are federal government agency representatives. 2 Our member organizations, including 13,000 enforcement officials, are dedicated to transportation safety and are committed to helping the Alliance achieve its goals of uniformity, compatibility and reciprocity of commercial motor vehicle inspections throughout North America. The Alliance works closely with federal regulators at the Department of Transportation’s Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) and the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration to advance our shared mission of reducing crashes, injuries and fatalities involving commercial motor vehicles on our shared roadways. CVSA leads the charge to increase knowledge of commercial motor vehicle operations and regulations and improve the comfort level of the motoring public through enforcement and education aimed at reducing fatalities and injuries on our roadways. CVSA developed and maintains the North American Standard Inspection Program, which is the roadside inspection process for inspecting commercial motor vehicles and drivers throughout North America. The program was developed to improve the safe operation of commercial motor vehicles by establishing a uniform and reciprocal roadside inspection and enforcement process. The program outlines inspection procedures, standards and requirements, and ensures consistency in compliance, inspections and enforcement, while minimizing duplication of efforts and unnecessary operating delays for the motor carrier industry. Using the North American Standard Inspection Program, approximately 4 million commercial motor vehicle inspections are conducted every year throughout North America by CVSA-certified inspectors to ensure the commercial motor vehicles on our roadways are operating safely. CVSA supports the stated goals of the proposed rule, which are to improve transparency, accountability and oversight for use of federal taxpayer dollars; clarify the status of OMB’s policies and requirements set forth in the 2 CFR regulatory text as an OMB regulation; and to reduce recipient burden. FMCSA administers several federal grant programs that fund the commercial motor vehicle safety programs implemented by the states and U.S. territories. The changes being proposed by OMB in the rule would directly impact the states and their safety programs, along with organizations, like CVSA, who support FMCSA and the states in their mission to reduce crashes, injuries and fatalities involving commercial motor vehicles. CVSA Comments to Proposed Rule 1.) Advertising and Public Relations [§ 200.421] OMB proposes to revise § 200.421 to specify that all advertising and public relations costs are unallowable with limited exceptions, including those required by statute, those related to the procurement of goods and services for the federal award, the disposal of certain scrap or surplus materials, or program outreach and other specific purposes necessary to meet the federal award requirements. CVSA is concerned that the language included in these proposed changes could be interpreted to mean that funds are not permitted to be spent on purchasing advertisement space/time for public service announcements that support the purpose of the award. Public service announcements are a standard tool used in many safety education and outreach programs and have been proven to be effective in changing driver behavior. In recognition of this, there is a long-established history of leveraging public service announcements, often in conjunction with high-visibility traffic enforcement, to raise the public’s awareness around a safety 3 message and, as a result, save lives. As written, the proposed language in § 200.241 would potentially limit the use of this powerful safety tool. To address this, CVSA encourages OMB to consider adding a fourth explicit exception for public service/educational messaging that supports the purpose of the award or clarifying that the exception in § 200.241(b)(3), as revised, includes public service/educational messaging that supports the purpose of the award. 2.) Conference Attendance [§ 200.432(b)] OMB is proposing to expand § 200.432(b) to add a requirement that the costs for attending conferences are allowable only if participation in the conference is expressly approved by the agency and included in the terms and conditions of the award. The revision would also clarify that recipients are not authorized to use federal funds to attend conferences that do not advance program outcomes. CVSA appreciates that OMB acknowledges that attendance at conferences and events can serve the purpose of the award and have value, and CVSA agrees that attendance at events and conferences funded by a federal award should advance the program outcomes. However, CVSA is concerned that the proposed language may be too restrictive and may inadvertently result in awardees being prohibited from participating in events and conferences that would bring value and serve the purpose of the award, largely because of process and timing. As currently written, § 200.432 already requires conference attendance to be necessary and reasonable for award performance. Adding additional, pre-approval requirements could create instances where awardees are prohibited from using federal funds to attend a conference that would otherwise be allowable, simply because the event details, such as date and location, are not available at the time the terms and conditions are issued. This is especially true for multi-year awards that may stretch several years into the future. The current requirements in § 200.432 provide the necessary oversight. However, if OMB determines it is necessary to proceed with changes, CVSA recommends allowing grant awards to be approved with a funds budgeted for travel to conferences and/or events to be identified later. The awardee could then be required to request agency approval for any unspecified travel that is identified after the terms and conditions are issued. This approach will address CVSA’s concern outlined above, while also ensuring the goal of the revision – improved oversight of the grant award – is met. 3.) Memberships, Subscriptions, and Professional Activity Costs [§ 200.454] a. Membership Dues [§ 200.454(a)] OMB is proposing to revise § 200.454(a) to limit eligibility of membership costs to only those that are necessary to fulfill the award requirements and only with prior written approval from the federal agency. CVSA supports including the exception for those instances where membership is “necessary to fulfill award requirements.” Government-based associations, like CVSA, exist to support government 4 employees in the execution of their responsibilities. In the wake of the deregulation of the motor carrier industry in the 1980s, the industry struggled with inconsistencies in enforcement practices and inspection procedures, resulting in wasted resources and increased costs for the transportation industry. CVSA was formed as a commitment by the jurisdictions and the motor carrier industry throughout North America to one another to develop and adhere to one standard commercial motor vehicle enforcement and inspection program – the North American Standard Inspection Program. The memorandum of understanding between the member jurisdictions, which serves as the foundation of the Alliance, was established to create uniformity and reciprocity in enforcement activities, outlining inspection procedures and out-of-service criteria. Participation in CVSA’s collective program is critical not just to its member jurisdictions, but to the motor carrier industry as well. CVSA appreciates that OMB’s proposed language rightly includes an exception for membership dues when, like in the case of CVSA, participation in the association is necessary for the state agencies that enforce the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations to apply the North American Standard Inspection Program. b. Subscriptions [200.454(b)] In addition, OMB proposes to revise § 200.454(b) to prohibit the use of federal funds on subscriptions to business, professional, academic and technical periodicals. CVSA requests that OMB reconsider this approach. Access to technical standards and various publications can be critical to effective implementation of an award’s purpose. For example, through a partnership with FMCSA and CVSA’s state, provincial, territorial and local members, CVSA provides education, training and awareness presentations and subject matter expert support related to commercial driver’s license (CDL) projects on a state and national level. In support of the “One Driver - One License - One Record” focus of the national CDL project, the Alliance supports FMCSA’s statement that the safety of America’s roadways depends on the public trust that every commercial driver has been rigorously verified and tested in strict accordance with federal regulations. Intentional or unintentional deviations from 49 CFR Parts 383 and 384, whether stemming from fraudulent testing schemes, insufficient oversight of third-party examiners, or compromised internal controls, undermine the foundation of the national CDL project. Additionally, uniform, consistent and accurate imposition of driver disqualifications, as required by the regulations, ensures that only those who meet strict safety, medical, and legal standards are allowed to operate CMVs. This subsequently relates to improving the corresponding accuracy and completeness of driver history records, including all conviction and disqualification data, medical certifications, entry-level driver training verification, and knowledge and skills testing information. The intended outcome of this project is to improve CMV safety through two activities which address the grant program’s focus of aiding states in their compliance efforts and improving the national CDL project. 5 As part of this initiative, CVSA maintains subscriptions to both West Law and Lexis-Nexis online databases, from which to cite current case law and legislative language necessary to address award deliverables. These resources are critical to CVSA’s ability to effectively meet the award requirements. Rather than prohibit subscriptions entirely, CVSA requests OMB consider taking an approach similar to that taken in other sections of the proposal; namely, to allow such expenses when necessary to fulfill the purpose of the grant award and only where pre-approved by the grantor agency. Such an approach would provide the intended oversight, while allowing the necessary flexibility to the agencies to authorize such expenses when they deem it necessary to fulfill the program’s purpose. Conclusion Oversight of the use of federal funds by recipients is an important responsibility of all federal agencies. CVSA supports the goals of the proposed rule, which are to improve transparency, accountability and oversight for use of federal taxpayer dollars; clarify the status of OMB’s policies and requirements set forth in the 2 CFR regulatory text as an OMB regulation; and to reduce recipient burden. As noted above, FMCSA administers several federal grant programs that fund the commercial motor vehicle safety programs implemented by the states and U.S. territories. The changes being proposed by OMB in the rule would directly impact the states and their safety programs, along with organizations, like CVSA, who support FMCSA and the states in their mission to reduce crashes, injuries and fatalities involving commercial motor vehicles. However, it is important that OMB ensure that the oversight measures are not overly restrictive, as that would have a negative impact on awardees’ ability to effectively meet stated program goals. This is particularly important when considering the many safety-related initiatives that the states implement, in part, with federal funds. CVSA encourages OMB to ensure that federal agencies retain the ability to approve the use of grant funds for various purposes, such as conference and event expenses and subscriptions to necessary technical standards and resources, so long as they align with the purpose of the grant program and are necessary for the awardee to complete their obligations under the federal award. CVSA works to closely monitor, evaluate and identify potentially unsafe transportation processes and procedures as well as to help facilitate and implement best practices for enhancing safety on our highways. Commercial motor vehicle safety continues to be a challenge and we need the involvement of all affected parties to help us better understand these issues and put into place practical solutions. We appreciate the opportunity to provide feedback to the agency. If you have further questions or comments, please do not hesitate to contact me at 202-998-1008 or collin.mooney@cvsa.org. Respectfully, Collin B. Mooney, MPA, CAE Executive Director Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance

text: I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of Management and Budget's proposed revisions to the Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards (Uniform Guidance). My comments are attached as Word document. I serve as President and Chief Executive Officer of LEADS Community Action Agency, a nonprofit organization headquartered in Newark, Ohio. For more than sixty years, LEADS has partnered with federal, state, and local governments to combat poverty through locally designed solutions. Today, we employ more than 120 people and administer a broad portfolio of federally funded programs, including Head Start and Early Head Start, the Community Services Block Grant (CSBG), the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP), Weatherization, affordable housing, and other initiatives that collectively serve approximately 15,000 households each year across central Ohio. --- ATTACHMENT CONTENT --- July 9, 2026 Andrew Reisig Joel Savary Office of Federal Financial Management U.S. Office of Management and Budget 725 17th Street, NW Washington, DC 20503 Re: Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance (OMB-2026-0034) Dear Mr. Reisig and Mr. Savary: I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of Management and Budget's proposed revisions to the Uniform Administrative Requirements, Cost Principles, and Audit Requirements for Federal Awards (Uniform Guidance). I serve as President and Chief Executive Officer of LEADS Community Action Agency, a nonprofit organization headquartered in Newark, Ohio. For more than sixty years, LEADS has partnered with federal, state, and local governments to combat poverty through locally designed solutions. Today, we employ more than 120 people and administer a broad portfolio of federally funded programs, including Head Start and Early Head Start, the Community Services Block Grant (CSBG), the Home Energy Assistance Program (HEAP), Weatherization, affordable housing, and other initiatives that collectively serve approximately 15,000 households each year across central Ohio. Our agency operates early childhood education centers serving more than 400 children, develops and manages more than 1,200 affordable housing units across two dozen Ohio counties, administers utility assistance and weatherization programs, and provides emergency services to individuals and families experiencing financial hardship. These responsibilities require us to manage numerous federal awards simultaneously while complying with extensive financial, programmatic, procurement, audit, and reporting requirements. In my role, I am ultimately responsible for ensuring our organization complies with the Uniform Guidance while also ensuring that the federal programs we administer achieve their intended outcomes for the communities we serve. Over the course of our history, LEADS has successfully managed millions of dollars in federal financial assistance while maintaining strong financial controls, complying with rigorous federal and state monitoring requirements, and consistently receiving clean independent financial and Single Audits. Our agency has successfully adapted to evolving federal regulations because we recognize that accountability and transparency are fundamental to maintaining public trust. The comments below should therefore not be interpreted as opposition to strong oversight. Rather, they reflect the perspective of an organization that has spent decades implementing federal programs and understands where regulations improve accountability and where they may unintentionally divert limited resources away from serving the public. I strongly support OMB's stated goals of improving accountability, increasing transparency, and reducing unnecessary administrative burden. Federal taxpayers deserve confidence that public dollars are managed responsibly, and nonprofit organizations entrusted with those resources should be held to high standards. At the same time, accountability is strengthened not simply by adding more requirements, but by establishing requirements that are clear, objective, practical, and consistently applied. Objective Standards Promote Better Compliance Several proposed provisions rely on subjective concepts such as "appearance," "reputational harm," "questionable practices," and "national interest." While I understand the intent behind these provisions, standards that depend upon interpretation rather than objective criteria create uncertainty for organizations attempting to operate in good faith. Our agency makes long-term commitments every time we accept a federal award. We hire teachers for Head Start classrooms, employ weatherization crews and energy auditors, execute construction contracts, lease facilities, and make investments in affordable housing developments that often require years to complete. These decisions require predictable regulatory expectations. Regulations should establish objective compliance standards that remain durable over the life of an award and across changes in administration. Administrative Requirements Should Produce Measurable Value Community Action Agencies already operate within one of the most highly regulated environments in the nonprofit sector. LEADS undergoes annual independent financial audits, Single Audits, federal and state program monitoring, licensing inspections, procurement reviews, internal control assessments, and extensive financial and performance reporting. Before additional reporting requirements or approval processes are imposed, I encourage OMB to carefully evaluate whether they meaningfully improve stewardship of taxpayer dollars or simply consume additional administrative resources. When reimbursement requests are delayed because of administrative processes, agencies must finance operations with limited working capital. When experienced staff spend additional hours preparing duplicative documentation, those are hours unavailable to enroll children in Head Start, assist seniors with utility assistance, help families avoid homelessness, or connect individuals with employment and housing resources. Administrative burden is not merely an operational inconvenience—it directly affects an organization's capacity to deliver services. Preserving Local Flexibility Strengthens Federal Programs One of the greatest strengths of the Community Action model is its ability to address poverty through locally developed solutions while remaining accountable for federally established outcomes. The needs of central Ohio differ from those of large metropolitan areas or other regions of the country. The Uniform Guidance has historically struck an appropriate balance by establishing strong accountability standards while allowing local organizations the flexibility necessary to respond to unique community needs. I encourage OMB to preserve that balance. Reconsider the Proposed Expansion of Discretionary Termination Authority I am particularly concerned about the proposed expansion of discretionary termination authority under § 200.340. Federal grant recipients make significant long-term commitments based upon approved awards. We hire employees, execute leases, enter into contracts, and make investments in facilities and infrastructure with the expectation that approved awards will continue throughout their designated performance periods. Broad termination authority based upon evolving priorities or undefined standards introduces uncertainty that discourages responsible long-term planning and investment. Ultimately, that uncertainty reduces stability for employees, nonprofit organizations, and the communities federal programs are intended to serve. If OMB retains expanded termination authority, I respectfully encourage the inclusion of clearly defined standards, robust notice requirements, meaningful opportunities for corrective action, and administrative appeal rights before awards may be suspended or terminated. Conclusion For more than six decades, LEADS has partnered with the federal government to help families move toward economic stability and self-sufficiency. We have done so under administrations of both political parties, through changing regulatory frameworks, and during periods of significant economic uncertainty. Throughout those changes, one principle has remained constant: clear, objective, and predictable regulations allow nonprofit organizations to focus their time and resources on delivering measurable results for the American people while maintaining responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars. I respectfully encourage OMB to finalize a Uniform Guidance that preserves strong accountability while recognizing the operational realities faced by organizations implementing federal programs in communities across the nation. The most effective regulations are those that hold recipients to high standards, provide clear expectations, eliminate unnecessary administrative burden, and preserve the flexibility needed for experienced local organizations to respond effectively to community needs. Thank you for considering these comments and for your continued commitment to improving the administration of federal financial assistance. Sincerely, Nathan J. Keirns President & Chief Executive Officer LEADS Community Action Agency

text: On behalf of the National Association of Flood & Stormwater Management Agencies (NAFSMA), we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) proposed rewrite of the Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR Part 200 and related parts, published May 29, 2026. NAFSMA represents flood control districts, stormwater utilities, state water agencies, and public works agencies nationwide that plan, build, and maintain the levees, floodwalls, pump stations, channels, and stormwater systems that protect millions of Americans. Our members are major recipients and subrecipients of federal financial assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and they administer that assistance under multi-year capital programs that frequently span three to seven years from design through construction. Please find our attached comments. --- ATTACHMENT CONTENT --- NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF FLOOD & STORMWATER MANAGEMENT AGENCIES (NAFSMA) P.O. Box 4336, Silver Spring, MD 20914 | Washington, DC (202) 289-8625 | www.nafsma.org July 9, 2026 Office of Federal Financial Management Office of Management and Budget Attn: Andrew Reisig and Joel Savary Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov Re: Comments on Proposed Rule, “Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance,” 91 FR 32198 (May 29, 2026); Docket No. OMB-2026-0034 Dear Director Vought: On behalf of the National Association of Flood & Stormwater Management Agencies (NAFSMA), we appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) proposed rewrite of the Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR Part 200 and related parts, published May 29, 2026. NAFSMA represents flood control districts, stormwater utilities, state water agencies, and public works agencies nationwide that plan, build, and maintain the levees, floodwalls, pump stations, channels, and stormwater systems that protect millions of Americans. Our members are major recipients and subrecipients of federal financial assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and they administer that assistance under multi-year capital programs that frequently span three to seven years from design through construction. We support OMB's stated goal of reducing recipient burden and appreciate that the proposal preserves the existing indirect cost rate negotiation system and limits agencies' ability to impose audit requirements beyond what federal statute authorizes. However, several other provisions would introduce new financial, legal, and administrative risk for public agencies delivering long-duration, capital-intensive flood risk reduction and water infrastructure projects. As instructed in the ADDRESSES section, we have organized our comments by the relevant section number. 1. Award Termination and Suspension Authority [§§ 200.211, 200.340–200.343] Expanded discretionary termination and suspension authority would allow a federal agency or pass-through entity to terminate an award, in whole or in part, whenever it determines termination is “in the interest of” the agency, including because an award no longer effectuates “the national interest as they exist at the time of the termination,” and to suspend an award for up to 90 days on the same standard — without a hearing or appeal right except in noncompliance-based terminations. The proposal exempts block grants, formula grants, and disaster recovery grants from discretionary termination, but does not extend that exemption to competitively awarded hazard mitigation programs such as FEMA's Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities (BRIC) program and Flood Mitigation Assistance (FMA) grants, or to EPA and USACE cooperative agreements. Flood control and stormwater infrastructure projects require years of design, permitting, and procurement before construction begins, and local sponsors routinely commit non-federal cost share, bond proceeds, and contractor obligations well before a project is complete. Mid-project termination without a right to be heard beforehand, or a guarantee that reasonably incurred costs and contractual commitments will be covered, exposes local governments to open-ended financial liability for infrastructure that may be partially built and could itself create a public safety hazard if abandoned. We recommend that OMB (a) extend the disaster recovery and formula grant exemption to competitively awarded flood risk reduction and water infrastructure programs, (b) require federal agencies to cover costs and contractual commitments reasonably incurred prior to a notice of termination, and (c) provide recipients an opportunity to respond before a discretionary termination is finalized, not only afterward. 2. Mid-Award Changes to Payment Terms and Conditions [§ 200.208] Authority to add, remove, or modify specific conditions during the period of performance — including switching a recipient from advance payments to reimbursement-only — creates cash-flow risk for public agencies financing multi-year construction contracts. A local flood district that budgeted and contracted for a project based on advance payment terms may not have the financial capacity to front months of construction draws if reimbursement is imposed mid-project. We recommend that any change from advance payment to reimbursement apply prospectively to new awards only, and that OMB require agencies to provide reasonable advance notice and a transition period before imposing new specific conditions on active construction projects with capital awards. 3. Subrecipient Monitoring and the “Reputational Damage” Standard [§§ 200.331, 200.332] The proposal's undefined “reputational damage” standard for terminating subawards adds significant uncertainty for NAFSMA members who receive FEMA and EPA funds as subrecipients through state pass-through entities. Because the term is not defined, a pass-through entity could be pressured to terminate a subaward for reasons unrelated to a subrecipient's actual performance or compliance. We recommend that OMB either remove this standard or replace it with an objective, documented noncompliance test consistent with the existing remedies for noncompliance at § 200.339. 4. Domestic Preference (Buy America) Requirements [§ 200.322] Strengthened domestic-preference requirements are appropriate in principle, but many components of flood control and stormwater infrastructure — large pumps, radial and sluice gates, SCADA and telemetry equipment, specialized geotextiles — have limited or no domestic manufacturing base. Tightening domestic-content requirements without a clear, timely waiver process risks delaying life-safety infrastructure such as levee pump stations and floodwalls. We ask OMB to preserve and clarify an accessible, predictable waiver process for components where domestic supply is unavailable or would cause unreasonable delay or cost, consistent with existing Build America, Buy America Act waiver practice. 5. Indirect Cost Rate Preference in Award Selection [§ 200.205] A stated preference, all else equal, for discretionary awards to applicants with lower indirect cost rates could disadvantage well-run public agencies whose negotiated indirect rates reflect legitimate engineering, permitting, and regulatory compliance overhead required to deliver federally funded infrastructure safely and in compliance with law. A lower indirect rate is not, by itself, a measure of program quality or delivery capacity. We ask OMB to clarify that this factor is not to be weighted in a way that disadvantages public agency applicants with properly negotiated indirect cost rates. In addition, another solution could be to put a cap on indirect costs as a percentage of construction costs. Encouraging agencies to reduce soft costs in award selections may lead to unintended perverse outcomes including inferior design, design short cuts and inspection processes that cost the public down the road. Those types of deficiencies aren’t necessarily visible for years. 6. Viewpoint-Neutrality Requirements for Events on Public Property [§ 200.219] The prohibition on “discriminatory event services” applies to events held on property under a recipient's control regardless of whether the specific event is federally funded which would impact public hearings, community flood-risk briefings, and levee certification meetings that flood control districts routinely hold on their own property. We ask OMB to clarify the scope of this provision so that public agencies can continue to manage public safety hearings and community meetings without uncertainty about compliance obligations that extend beyond the federally funded activity itself. 7. E-Verify Mandate [§§ 200.303, 200.318] The new requirement that recipients and subrecipients participate in E- Verify adds a new compliance obligation that will flow down through multiple tiers of a typical flood infrastructure award — state pass-through entity, local district, and construction contractors and subcontractors. We ask OMB to clarify flow-down responsibility so verification is not duplicated at every tier, and to provide a reasonable phase-in period so public agencies and their existing construction contracts can come into compliance without disrupting active capital projects. 8. Multi-Year Awards and Notice of Funding Opportunity Reform [§§ 200.202, 200.204] NAFSMA supports the proposal's encouragement of multi-year awards with budget periods longer than one year and plain-language, predictably posted notices of funding opportunities. Flood control and stormwater infrastructure projects rarely fit within a single-year budget period. We encourage OMB to expressly extend multi-year award authority to FEMA hazard mitigation and EPA water infrastructure grant programs, which would meaningfully reduce administrative burden for both agencies and recipients. 9. Implementation Timeline Finally, we are concerned about the overall implementation timeline. A rulemaking of this scope — with a 45- day comment period ending July 13, 2026, and a proposed effective date of October 1, 2026 — leaves public agencies very little lead time to update procurement policies, subaward agreements, and internal controls before the start of federal fiscal year 2027. We recommend a phased effective date for provisions requiring new operational systems or contract changes (including E-Verify, payment justification, and SAM.gov subaward reporting compliance), particularly for public agencies already managing multi-year capital programs with contracts in active procurement. Conclusion NAFSMA appreciates OMB's effort to modernize and clarify the rules governing federal financial assistance, and we share the goal of ensuring taxpayer dollars are managed responsibly. We ask that OMB consider the practical realities of financing and delivering multi-year, capital-intensive flood risk reduction and stormwater infrastructure when finalizing this rule. NAFSMA and our member agencies are glad to serve as a resource on these issues as the rulemaking proceeds. Please contact me at sunny@nafsma.org or (202) 289-8625 with any questions. Sincerely, Sunny Simpkins Executive Director National Association of Flood & Stormwater Management Agencies (NAFSMA)
