text: See attached file(s) --- ATTACHMENT CONTENT --- MEMO: Comment on Rules Changes to 2 CFR 200 From: Open Research Funders Group Date: 13 July 2026 Please consider the attached as a formal response to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Proposed rules changes to 2 CFR 200 - Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance. This response addresses only one portion of the proposed rules changes, based on our collective expertise and experience: Section 200.461—Publication and Printing Costs. Although this comment only focuses on §200.461, OMB should clarify that §200.454 does not destabilize institutional library access or infrastructure needed for federally funded research Open Research Funders Group (ORFG) is a coalition of private philanthropic funders committed to the open sharing of research outputs. Collectively, ORFG members hold assets in excess of $200 billion, with total annual grantmaking in the $22 billion range. We believe openness is better for the American public, better for research, better for global society, and better for philanthropy. Open research accelerates the pace of discovery, reduces information-sharing gaps, encourages innovation, and promotes reproducibility. As members of the private philanthropic community, we strive to support the rapid and wide dissemination of scientific outputs that serve our society. This community uses a variety of strategies and approaches to increase scientific discovery and continuously works to improve the scientific ecosystem. We have knowledge and expertise in funding scientific outputs – such as preprints, datasets, code and tangible materials – as well as assessing their impacts. Much like the Administration, we are deeply concerned with the high costs of publication, and support federal action to reduce individual publication costs. Currently, most of these costs are captured under Article Processing Charges (APCs) – publisher-imposed fees to make publicly funded research publicly available. These fees, paid with American taxpayers’ dollars, largely support for-profit publishers whose revenues have skyrocketed as a result of these fee impositions. For example, in Q1 2026, Springer Nature saw increases of 7.2% growth driven by its journals portfolio, which is ORFG Comment on Rules Changes to 2 CFR 200 - July 2026​ 1 seeing increasing adoption of open access models relying on APCs.1 The journal Nature demands an exorbitant APC of $12,850 per article.2 A recent report by the International Network for Advancing Science and Policy (INASP) estimated the cumulative APC costs for 21 global development funders to be between $74 million and $81 million total.3 Moreover, the report concludes, "The amounts invested by research funders in open access publication are not translating into all their funded research outputs being immediately available to everyone. There is potential for this money to be reinvested in open, sustainable, and equitable publishing models for the future.”4 Estimated federal taxpayer dollars spent on APCs rose from $281 million in 2016 to $399 million in 2022–a $118 million increase in 6 years.5 As a response to the ineffectiveness of APCs, several private funders limit or prohibit funding of publication costs, including but not limited to Astera Institute, Navigation Fund, Gates Foundation, and Howard Hughes Medical Institute. At the same time other funders are in the process of limiting or prohibiting publication costs. This number is increasing.6 Many private philanthropic funders require or strongly encourage the immediate deposit of preprints into repositories alongside other research outputs such as data, tangible materials, code, and more. Using these mechanisms to share scientific outputs allows for rapid sharing at lower individual costs. These funders include: Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Aligning Science Across Parkinson’s, Gates Foundation, Alex’s Lemonade Stand, the Simons Foundation, Wellcome Trust, Arcadia Fund, Michael J. Fox 6 Open Research Funders Group, ORFG Funder Policy Landscape Report and Recommendations: 2026 (Zenodo, 2026), https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20451484. 5 Updated Report to the U.S. Congress on Financing Mechanisms for Open Access Publishing of Federally Funded Research (Office of Science and Technology Policy, 2024), https://bidenwhitehouse.archives.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/2024-Report-to-Appropriations-Committee-on -Scholarly-Publishing-and-Public-Access-Implementation.pdf. 4 Chadwick El-Ali et al., A Review of Open Access Policy Options for Development Research Funders | INASP. 3 Alice Chadwick El-Ali et al., A Review of Open Access Policy Options for Development Research Funders | INASP (INASP, 2025), https://www.inasp.info/open-access-policy-options-paper. 2 “Publishing Options | Nature,” accessed June 11, 2026, https://www.nature.com/nature/for-authors/publishing-options. 1 “Strong Research Segment Helps Springer Nature to Increased Q1 Profits,” Research Information, May 5, 2026, https://www.researchinformation.info/news/strong-research-segment-helps-springer-nature-to-increased-q1-profit s/; “Springer Nature Reports Growth in Submissions, Usage and OA Publishing,” Research Information, March 31, 2026, https://www.researchinformation.info/news/springer-nature-reports-growth-in-submissions-usage-and-oa-publish ing/. ORFG Comment on Rules Changes to 2 CFR 200 - July 2026​ 2 Foundation, Moore Foundation, and Templeton World Charity Foundation. For a matrix of some funders' approaches to preprints, visit the Preprint Policy Framework developed by Creative Commons and hosted by ASAPbio.7 At the same time, private philanthropy cannot and should not be treated as a replacement payer for federal public-access obligations. Eliminating direct individual publication costs is one way to approach a broader problem. We are in support of eliminating individual publication costs (APCs, page and color charges, etc.), however, we remain concerned that the commercial publishing industry will invent new revenue streams that generate more barriers to the rapid dissemination of openly shared research outputs. As such, OMB should also provide a transition period for nonprofit, society, university, and community-governed publishing venues that lack the flexibility to absorb sudden changes in federal cost policy. This will allow them to remain competitive and viable in today’s market. The fundamental issue is that publishing and evaluation systems are bundled with the sharing of scientific outputs, which hampers the ability for the public to easily access taxpayer-funded research in a timely manner. No longer is article publication the only means to share research outputs. Scientific dissemination is not ancillary to federally funded research. It is part of the research lifecycle. Publications, preprints, datasets, code, protocols, software, metadata, persistent identifiers, and curated repositories are the mechanisms by which research is validated, reproduced, reused, and translated into public benefit. A rule intended to reduce excessive APCs should not sweep in the infrastructure and services necessary to make research outputs openly available, machine-readable, and reusable. To relieve the publishing costs burdening the American public, sharing scientific outputs should be unbundled from the traditional publishing and evaluation system of formal publication. Instead, policies should require the immediate sharing and licensing to allow reuse research outputs in the form of preprints, data deposit, code sharing, and more. The cost savings from publication and printing charges could then be repurposed to robust open science infrastructure such as preprint servers and code repositories, which–when appropriately funded–entails a substantially smaller financial investment than the roughly $400 million spent by the federal government on article processing charges per year. Moreover, it provides a robust, open science landscape that will accelerate the 7 Advancing Openly Licensed Preprints: Aligning Across A Standard Preprints Policy Framework – ASAPbio, July 16, 2025, https://asapbio.org/preprint-policy-framework/. ORFG Comment on Rules Changes to 2 CFR 200 - July 2026​ 3 sharing of scientific findings and increase transparency in the research and funding ecosystem. Robust open science infrastructures already exist and are being used and embraced by the scientific community. Examples include numerous preprint servers and repositories that host taxpayer-funded datasets, code, and other materials. These repositories rely on open licensing and quality metadata standards that allow for machine readability and interoperability, ensuring that learning models can access and retrieve scientific outputs. In turn, this will make way for future innovations in scientific communication, ending our reliance on the broken publishing system. Funding open access infrastructure that supports the rapid dissemination of research findings is paramount for improving science and making taxpayer-funded research more accessible to the public. OMB should consider shifting its focus from the traditional publishing system to supporting the continued development and adoption of open science infrastructures that can serve as dissemination systems. By sharing data, preprints, tangible materials, and code, scientists can more rapidly build on research findings to accelerate future innovations. This model still allows for formal publication, but decouples formal publication from research sharing and research evaluation. Thank you for your efforts to study the scientific publication costs problem and for your dedication to improving the rapidity of sharing scientific outputs. We welcome deeper conversations with the OMB as it tackles this important problem and makes science openly available to the public. ORFG Comment on Rules Changes to 2 CFR 200 - July 2026​ 4

text: Please see the attached comments from Itron regarding domestic manufacturing. --- ATTACHMENT CONTENT --- 1 Itron Inc. Dan Pfeiffer Vice President of Government and Regulatory Affairs 2111 N Molter Road Liberty Lake, WA 99019 July 13, 2026 The Honorable Russell Vought Director Office of Management and Budget 725 17th Street, NW Washington, D.C. 20503 RE: Itron Comments on Docket OMB-2026-0034 Sent via the Federal eRulemaking Portal Dear Director Vought: Itron appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments on the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) proposed rule entitled Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance, revising the Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance (Uniform Guidance), 2 CFR Part 200. As a U.S.-based company manufacturing state-of-the-art grid management solutions in the U.S. – including advanced metering technologies and technologies that support utility system reliability – Itron is deeply committed to expanding grid capacity through American-made solutions. Our continued investment in domestic manufacturing not only strengthens the nation’s energy infrastructure but also supports thousands of high-quality U.S. jobs. By maintaining and modernizing our American manufacturing facilities, Itron helps build a skilled workforce, promotes economic growth in the communities where we operate, and ensures that the benefits of American energy dominance are felt by American workers and their families. With approximately 1,500 jobs at Itron’s U.S. manufacturing facility, Itron supports Buy America provisions and the Administration’s vision for transformational investments in the nation’s grid. To that end, Itron encourages OMB to consider the further use of a “substantial transformation” standard for advanced grid technologies’ compliance with Buy America requirements. Substantial Transformation Proposal We appreciate the Administration’s commitment to American energy dominance and domestic manufacturing through adherence to federal Buy America requirements. 2 As noted in § 200.322 (Domestic Preferences for Procurements), a key element of federal funding programs is the application of Buy America requirements. Itron supports Buy America programs and has had extensive experience with the challenges posed in supply chains, development of domestic manufacturing and integrated manufacturing processes. Within Buy America programs, there has been a long-time recognition of a “substantial transformation” standard1 as part of determining compliance with domestic content requirements. Effective application of a substantial transformation standard for advanced grid technologies’ compliance with Buy America requirements is a critical necessity within federal funding programs, particularly at the Department of Energy (DOE). Buy America requirements boost American manufacturing and enable economic growth; however, the way these domestic content requirements are interpreted by individual federal agencies could delay critical infrastructure upgrades for years. Our energy grid urgently requires modernization and upgrades to keep pace with growing energy demand due to technological advances such as AI and national security priorities. It is essential to both economic and national security that the Administration's interpretation of what it means to be “Made in America” aligns with these objectives. Our federal government, including during the first Trump Administration, has long recognized manufacturing processes that substantially transform components into a final manufactured product for use under funding programs and government acquisition as compliant with Buy America standards. These policies and regulations are a necessary reflection of the value and importance of substantial transformation to domestic manufacturing and innovation. Substantial transformation counts any manufactured good as domestic if it has been substantially transformed in the U.S. into something distinct from its imported components and subcomponents. The substantial transformation test is rigorous and requires that the domestic manufacturing process be complex and meaningful, ensuring that American products are made in American factories by highly skilled American workers. Most domestic smart grid edge systems are made in America. However, their supply chains rely on a wide network of global sources for thousands of small components, many of which – such as resistors and capacitors – can cost less than one cent each and are predominantly manufactured abroad. American companies then integrate these parts into innovative grid edge technologies that are unquestionably designed, engineered, and manufactured in the U.S. 1 See U.S. Dep’t of Com., Int’l Trade Admin., Rules of Origin: Substantial Transformation, https://www.trade.gov/rules-origin-substantial-transformation. See also Trade Agreements Act of 1979,19 U.S.C. § 2518(4)(B). See also 2 CFR § 176.160(a). 3 It is important to recognize that, even with prioritization of domestic sourcing and manufacturing processes, there remain some components that go into smart grid edge technologies that are not currently available from domestic sources. Rebuilding the domestic supply chain for every individual component is not feasible in the near term and penalizing domestic manufacturers of advanced smart grid edge technologies will result in unnecessary delays and risks to the stability and modernization of the electric grid: a national security priority. We strongly support the Administration’s goal of revitalizing our domestic industry and reducing dependence on foreign sources for strategic technologies. Given enough time, a 55% domestic content requirement for advanced grid edge technologies is achievable, if we fully value existing manufacturing jobs that substantially transform components into final products. Reaching this goal, however, requires an approach that acknowledges the current complexity of global supply chains, particularly in sectors as specialized as the smart grid. Realizing gains in domestic manufacturing and ensuring our national energy security through a modernized grid are mutually important goals that require a balanced approach. The Trump Administration’s objectives to bolster domestic supply chains and expand American manufacturing jobs are crucial. At the same time, applying an inflexible domestic content requirement on grid edge technology manufactured products, particularly one that does not consider substantial transformation, poses an immediate risk to achieving these objectives. We urge the Office of Management and Budget to reaffirm and ensure that agencies apply the substantial transformation standard to federal assistance and acquisition programs supporting advanced grid edge technologies. In particular, it is critical to count products that are substantially transformed in the U.S. from imported components as domestically manufactured for the purposes of compliance with 2 CFR 200 and 2 CFR 184. Complex global supply chains, particularly in the highly specialized smart grid sector, cannot be rebuilt overnight. As a result, application of domestic content requirements without recognition of the domestic manufacturing through substantial transformation overlooks the vital contributions of American engineers, technicians, and factory workers.

[200.461] — Publication and Printing Costs Risk to U.S. global leadership The United States’ leadership in science depends not only on conducting research but on its independent validation and on rapidly and widely communicating results. Other countries, like China, are expanding investments in open science and publication infrastructure and as we write today, China is now out-investing America in all areas of science and technology. China’s research output has risen 22.4% from 2024 to 2025.1 China is also producing a growing number of scientific publications and patents, signaling both scale and momentum. The proposed constraint by OMB risks slowing U.S. research visibility and weakening its international competitiveness even further. Banning publication costs may yield marginal short-term savings for the U.S. government, but would ultimately impose far greater long-term costs as the U.S. continues to fall behind China in scientific investment. Publication is mischaracterized as optional rather than integral The proposal rests on the mistaken premise that publication costs are “not inherently necessary” to the core objectives of most Federal awards. This framing is inconsistent with decades of Federal research policy as well as the recent agency public access policies, under which dissemination of findings is a fundamental component of the research lifecycle that drives scientific progress, improves lives, and fuels economic growth. Peer-review enabled by the publication process is not a discretionary add-on; it is the primary mechanism by which scientific results are validated, duplication of effort is minimized, and public and private sector innovation is enabled. This is at the heart of Gold Standard Science. We support OMB's goal to maximize the value of each research grant. However, the value and impact of agency-funded research can’t be fully realized without impactful journals that amplify and provide access to the latest scientific discoveries in the form of articles, data, code and other supplementary materials that make the science reproducible and trusted. Publication and dissemination of research is what delivers a full return on the taxpayer’s investment. Without access to the trusted, peer-reviewed publication, trust, public impact, and economic return will be undermined. The vast majority of research submitted for publication is conceived and performed with honesty, rigor, and care, helping to advance scientific progress. But as the volume 1 Nature. (2026, June 10). Nature Index 2026 Research Leaders rankings: Are China’s East Asian neighbors keeping pace with it? https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-026-01662-x and complexity of academic research grows, so do the challenges of safeguarding the integrity of the published record. Predatory journals, paper mills, inappropriate use of AI-generated content, and "publish or perish" incentive structures threaten the integrity of the scientific record. In the face of these challenges Springer Nature has maintained the highest standards of submission, evaluation, peer-review, editorial assessment and article acceptance. Our average article acceptance rates for all journals have steadily declined in the face of these pressures. But lower acceptance rates do not mean less work; in fact, they mean the opposite, and this extra work has to be funded from the income generated from what is published. As the volume and sophistication of threats to research integrity grow, our declining acceptance rates demonstrate that our rigorous editorial and peer-review processes are successfully filtering out unreliable, fraudulent, or otherwise unsuitable papers. Springer Nature takes these threats and responsibilities seriously and has invested accordingly. In general, U.S.-funded research achieves a standard of quality that merits global recognition and impact, and researchers need appropriate channels of dissemination to help achieve that. American researchers are best positioned to choose the most appropriate journals that reach their target audience and achieve scientific and wider impact. Researchers need a broad range of publication options to share everything from incremental advances and null results to paradigm-shifting discoveries of the greatest significance. At Springer Nature, we support a wide portfolio of journals that provide the variety, flexibility, and support that U.S.-funded researchers require. Preventing the recovery of publication costs except in narrow circumstances effectively severs the final, essential step of federally funded research to enable other U.S. researchers to confidently and efficiently build on their work and avoid much higher duplicate costs and inefficiencies. The proposal conflicts with Gold Standard Science (GSS) goals The GSS Implementation Plan will be significantly undermined by disallowing publication costs. Under current grant guidance, Springer Nature is well positioned to partner with the U.S. government to advance research integrity, transparency, reproducibility, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the accessibility of research at scale. For example, many of our journals and our preprint server have been publishing negative results and replication studies for many years. Negative results are not failures. They are a key means of science self-correcting, helping researchers avoid paths proven not to work, and saving American taxpayers time and money. In addition, good communication of research acknowledges competing interests and is reproducible, transparent, judicious, collaborative, able to be tested and challenged, unbiased, and inclusive of negative results. Publishers’ editors and peer reviewers work with scientists to ensure all this is done. The resulting articles benefit greatly from the quality assurance, corrections, additions to the article and the widespread added value dissemination services that committed publishers like Springer Nature provide. Springer Nature, along with others in scientific publishing, has invested substantially— and continues to invest—to meet the goals of the upcoming U.S. GSS Implementation Plan. These goals would be severely undermined by the OMB proposal. Administrative burden and inefficiency The requirement for case-by-case prior approval will impose substantial administrative burdens on federal agencies, recipients and subrecipients, and publication partners. Given the volume of federally funded outputs annually, at an average of a quarter million publications a year,2 this process is not scalable. It will slow publication timelines, create inefficiencies and cost duplication, increase transactional costs, create uncertainty for budgeting and project planning, and divert resources away from scientific work. Moreover, publication costs are already well-understood, standardized, and auditable in most contexts. The proposal replaces a predictable framework with fragmented and inconsistent approval processes, undermining OMB’s stated goal of consistency. Disproportionate impact on early-career researchers and rural institutions Restricting allowability will particularly harm early-career researchers without access to other discretionary funds and smaller universities and nonprofits, particularly those located in rural areas. This pipeline, particularly of early-career researchers, is absolutely vital to the continued competitive standing and economic viability of the United States. Larger institutions may be able to absorb publication costs internally; many others cannot. The result will be reduced participation in dissemination and diminished visibility of federally funded work in all corners of the country, weakening the output of American science. [200.454] — Memberships, Subscriptions, and Professional Activity Costs Subscriptions and memberships are essential research infrastructure The proposal would render subscriptions to academic and technical periodicals unallowable and require prior approval for memberships necessary to fulfill award requirements. Access to scholarly literature is not discretionary—it is foundational to the undertaking and creation of research. Researchers must survey prior work, rely on 2 Schares, E. (2023). Impact of the 2022 OSTP memo: A bibliometric analysis of U.S. federally funded publications, 2017–2021. Quantitative Science Studies, 4(1), 1–21. https://doi.org/10.1162/qss_a_00237 and build on it where appropriate, ensure novelty, interpret results in context, and comply with standards of rigor and reproducibility. Without access to journals, databases, and professional organizations, researchers cannot effectively perform federally funded work. Tension with the publication restriction The combined effect of §§ 200.461 and 200.454 creates a systemic contradiction: • researchers may not recover costs to publish their work, • and may not recover costs to access others’ work that may not be publicly accessible. This dual restriction undermines the entire knowledge exchange ecosystem, impairing both input (literature access) and output (publication). These processes are often time- sensitive and integral to ongoing research. The added friction will reduce efficiency and innovation, increase costs, and reduce the competitiveness of U.S. science, effectively dismantling the mechanisms that have long sustained America’s storied history of scientific leadership. Recommendations We respectfully recommend that OMB: 1. Retain allowability of publication costs as a standard, not exceptional, expense because dissemination is a core programmatic objective of research awards, consistent with longstanding Federal policy. 2. Withdraw the blanket prohibition on subscriptions to enable U.S. researchers to efficiently build on the validated work of others. 3. Eliminate prior approval requirements to avoid administrative burden and bottlenecks. 4. Provide a minimum 90-day comment period given the breadth, complexity, and far-reaching implications of these transformative proposed revisions. Conclusion The proposed changes would disrupt the core mechanisms through which federally funded research is validated, disseminated, accessed, and applied. By restricting both publication and access, the intended rule changes risk diminishing the return on Federal research investments, weakening the U.S. research ecosystem, and critically undermining the legacy and continuation of America’s global scientific leadership. We urge OMB to revise the proposal to allow publication costs to support—not constrain—the full lifecycle of research, from discovery through dissemination and impact for a stronger America.

text: I strongly oppose the proposed changes in OMB Docket OMB-2026-0034 that would allow senior political appointees to have the final authority over federal grant awards following scientific or technical peer review. The strength of the federal grant system has long depended on decisions being driven primarily by merit, technical excellence, and public benefit rather than by changing political priorities. Making peer review merely advisory risks undermining confidence that awards are based on objective evaluation. Moreover, the idea of overriding reviews and recommendations by persons who are not scientists and who, by definition, are politically motivated renders this administration’s so-called “Gold Standard Science” (Executive Order #14303) a joke. I urge OMB to pay particular attention to item 7 in the definition of “Gold Standard Science”: “Subject to unbiased peer review”. Career program officials and independent expert reviewers possess the subject-matter expertise necessary to evaluate the scientific, technical, and societal merits of complex proposals. Political appointees are accountable for implementing an administration’s policy objectives, but they should not replace expert judgment in determining which individual proposals represent the highest-quality investments. Allowing political officials to overrule peer review without clear, objective standards creates the appearance—and potentially the reality—of political influence in funding decisions. Federal research and other grant programs have earned international respect because they are viewed as merit-based, predictable, and insulated from partisan considerations. Weakening that foundation could discourage talented investigators, reduce public trust in federal funding decisions, and ultimately diminish the quality and impact of federally supported research and public programs. I respectfully urge OMB to revise the proposed rule to preserve independent peer review as the primary basis for grant selection and to limit political review to ensuring legal and procedural compliance rather than making the final funding decision.

text: My great niece has been battling cancer since she was three years old. After being cancer free for ten years, she became symtamatic in her early teens and survived relapsed acute lymphoblastic leukemia. After her cancer returned, she underwent intensive treatment, including a bone marrow transplant from an unrelated donor. Following her transplant, she developed graft-versus-host disease, a serious and potentially life-threatening complication. Fortunately, she was able to receive a newer targeted therapy that helped control her disease and quash the GVHD. Years ago, treatment options would have been far less advanced. And perhaps a different outcome would have been the result. I am concerned about the proposed revisions to §§200.202, 200.204, 200.205, 200.218, 200.300, 200.340, and 200.432. As I understand them, federally funded programs would be expected to align with Administration priorities and politics would have a deeper role in science and research decisions. When a life threatening illness strikes a family member, no one asks whether a treatment aligned with the priorities of a particular Administration when the research was funded. What matters is whether the science was rigorous and whether researchers were allowed to pursue important questions. Scientific breakthroughs often emerge decades after the original research is funded. If funding decisions become tied to changing political priorities, future discoveries may never be realized. The strength of the American research system has been its commitment to funding the best science and allowing experts to determine which questions are most important to pursue. I respectfully urge OMB to withdraw the proposed changes to §§200.202, 200.204, 200.205, 200.218, 200.300, 200.340, and 200.432. Families facing serious illnesses depend on a research system that is transparent, stable, collaborative, and guided by scientific expertise. Funding decisions should be based on scientific merit and the potential to improve lives, not shifting political priorities. The treatments that saved my great niece’s life are proof of what is possible when science is allowed to follow the evidence and when taxpayer investments are allowed to realize their full potential. Please consider keeping politics out of federally funded research programs and leave science to the experts.

text: As a practicing pathologist, I urge the Office of Management and Budget to withdraw the proposed rule, "Rule to Revise the Guidance for Federal Financial Assistance" (Docket OMB-2026-0034). The federal government should protect the value of federally funded research by preserving rigorous peer review decisions and independent scientific inquiry. Pathologists rely on high-quality, evidence-based research every day to diagnose disease, guide treatment decisions, and improve patient outcomes. Much of the scientific evidence that informs pathology and laboratory medicine is made possible by federally funded research that is evaluated through an established peer review process based on scientific merit and expertise. While I support efforts to improve transparency, accountability, and stewardship of taxpayer dollars, I am concerned that several provisions in the proposed rule would undermine these objectives. Policies that allow research funding decisions to be influenced by factors other than scientific merit, expand the authority to terminate awards after they have been made, and weaken independent peer review could reduce confidence in federally funded research and discourage scientific innovation. The proposed rule has implications that extend far beyond individual research grants. If the changes are implemented, they would undermine the future of US biomedical research, the development of new diagnostic tools, careers in medicine and research, and ultimately the quality of care available to people in the US. Maintaining a predictable, objective, and merit-based research funding process is essential to preserving the United States' leadership in medical research and ensuring continued advances in pathology and laboratory medicine. Given the breadth and complexity of these proposed changes, I urge OMB to abandon the October 1, 2026 implementation plan and engage with affected stakeholders prior to finalizing a new proposal. Changes of this magnitude deserve careful consideration and meaningful input from the scientific and medical communities. I respectfully urge OMB to withdraw the proposed rule, maintain rigorous peer review, protect independent scientific inquiry, and ensure that federal research funding continues to prioritize scientific excellence while promoting transparency, accountability, and responsible stewardship of public resources. Thank you for considering my comments.

Organizations should not have to question whether their eligibility for funding may change because of shifting political priorities unrelated to their performance or the needs of the communities they serve. Organizations that advocate for survivors, educate policymakers, or work to improve public systems must be able to fulﬁll their missions without concern that legitimate advocacy or collaboration could jeopardize their federal funding. The Uniform Guidance has historically provided consistent government-wide standards that promote transparency, accountability, and eﬀective stewardship of federal funds. The proposed revisions move away from these principles by introducing uncertainty into every stage of the grant lifecycle—from application and award through implementation and closeout. Rather than strengthening grant administration, these changes would make it more diﬃcult for nonproﬁt organizations to focus their resources on serving communities. For these reasons, NDDSVC respectfully urges the Oﬃce of Management and Budget to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule. Federal grant regulations should preserve fairness, transparency, due process, and predictability while maintaining strong ﬁnancial accountability. Organizations serving victims and survivors should be able to rely on stable grant administration so they can focus on their mission of providing safety, advocacy, and hope to those experiencing violence. Thank you for considering these comments and for your commitment to improving federal grant administration in a manner that supports both accountability and eﬀective community services. Sincerely, Seth O'Neill, JD, MSW Executive Director North Dakota Domestic & Sexual Violence Coalition

text: [200.205, 200.340, 200.341, 200.432, 200.454, 200.461] I am writing in my personal capacity to voice my strong opposition to this proposed rule, as it would cause significant harm to the scientific community and signal an abdication of US leadership in the sciences. I am especially concerned by the following sections of the rule: Section 200.205: By making peer review advisory and mandating that senior political appointees review discretionary awards to ensure alignment with shifting political priorities, this rule introduces unprecedented political interference into scientific funding. The peer review system, a process widely regarded as the gold standard for evaluating scientific merit and funding decisions, is built on the rigorous evaluation of proposals by independent scientific experts. This ensures that funding decisions are based on mission-driven scientific innovation and potential impact - not political considerations, which is why the U.S. has consistently led the way in driving breakthrough research and accelerating technological innovation. Shifting final authority to political appointees will significantly undermine the grant review and award system and could distort federal research priorities based on ideological or partisan agendas, stifle innovation, and erode public confidence in research. Research should focus on scientific inquiry, promise, and innovation to advance science and improve public health above politics. Sections 200.340 and 200.341: The new grant termination authorities introduced in these sections could introduce significant instability for long-term scientific projects. Allowing federal agencies to terminate or suspend active, multi-year grants mid-project for broad, subjective reasons—such as a shift in agency priorities or "national interest" determinations—undermines the security needed to conduct cutting-edge research. In fields like astronomy, projects rely on years of continuous data collection, graduate student training, and stable collaboration. Canceling grants midstream due to ever-shifting agency priorities would squander investments already committed to facilities, equipment, and specialized personnel, reducing our return on federal spending and potentially undermining the principle of accepting negative results as positive outcomes. Further, permitting awards to be terminated for reasons unrelated to performance or compliance opens the door for administrations of either party to effectively end funding for lines of research deemed politically sensitive. Employing such terminations will create perverse incentives to align research results with political agendas. The constant threat of arbitrary cancellations will stifle innovation, discourage high-risk, high-reward research, and severely damage the retention of scientific talent, undercutting U.S. competitiveness in a global research environment where other countries offer more predictable funding streams. Sections 200.432, 200.454, and 200.461: The proposed rule will also place undue restrictions on collaboration that will isolate American scientists and stifle innovation. Presumptively treating conference costs, professional society memberships, and publishing costs as unallowable is overly restrictive and will only harm our community's ability to steward meaningful, high-reward science. Forcing researchers to navigate a political approval gauntlet just to share data at a conference or publish a peer-reviewed paper creates immense administrative burdens and isolates U.S. research. I strongly urge OMB to withdraw these damaging provisions and protect the non-partisan, merit-driven nature of federal research funding.

The proposal to replace the time-tested scientific peer-review process with funding decisions made by political appointees, combined with the provision allowing research grants to be canceled mid-study, represents a fundamental threat to the American scientific enterprise. If finalized, this rule will deeply politicize scientific research, undermine public health, and halt critical medical breakthroughs before they can even begin. For decades, the United States has led global innovation precisely because our scientific funding mechanisms have relied on objective, merit-based peer review. When experts in biology, epidemiology, engineering, and physics evaluate grant proposals, they ensure that taxpayer dollars are allocated to research with the highest technical merit, rigorous methodologies, and maximum potential for societal benefit. Replacing these independent experts with political appointees shifts the criteria for funding from empirical potential to ideological alignment. Science relies on unbiased inquiry; injecting partisan politics into the selection process ensures that vital research on public health, climate, and medicine will be suppressed if its potential findings clash with a prevailing political agenda. Furthermore, the provision allowing grants to be arbitrarily canceled mid-study introduces severe instability into the scientific community. Scientific discovery—particularly the development of life-saving drugs or long-term epidemiological tracking—requires years of sustained, uninterrupted funding. Allowing political figures to abruptly pull the plug on active research wastes millions of taxpayer dollars already invested, leaves critical studies half-finished, and dismantles the multi-year collaborative pipelines required to achieve breakthroughs. It also creates a chilling effect, discouraging our nation’s brightest minds from pursuing high-stakes, long-term research out of fear that their life's work could be erased by a change in political winds. Ultimately, this proposed rule will break public trust in federal institutions. When the public can no longer be certain that government-funded science is objective and insulated from political manipulation from either party, trust in health guidelines, regulatory approvals, and safety standards collapses. The health of our citizens, the strength of our economy, and our standing as a global leader in innovation depend entirely on independent, evidence-based science. I urge the Office of Management and Budget to immediately withdraw this deeply damaging proposal and instead work to protect and strengthen the integrity of the peer-review process. Sincerely, Sara Brown

I write as a concerned citizen who cares about the wellbeing of the children, women, and men of this great country. This proposed rule is not a grants management reform. It is the most consequential attack on American science and on the integrity of federal grantmaking since WWII. It would place political appointees above scientific peer reviewers in every grant funding decision, allow any active grant to be terminated mid-project for undefined political reasons, prohibit international scientific collaboration, ban journal subscriptions and publication costs that have been allowable for over fifty years, and require that every federal grant program align with the current administration’s political priorities rather than with scientific need or congressional mandate. I fully trust scientists who have dedicated their lives to their field over a political appointee, who may not have any education or training in the fields of study, to make these decision. Scientific peer review is the primary protection against waste, fraud, and abuse in federal science funding. Replacing it with political review does not improve stewardship of federal funds. It eliminates the most rigorous quality control mechanism federal science has. This overtly puts politics over serving what is best for the American people. §200.340 — Discretionary termination on undefined “national interest” grounds The American people deserve to know the definition of “national interest” when grant funding for potentially life saving research is on the line. The opacity of this section does not serve the American people. §200.421 and §200.450 — Public communications and issue advocacy prohibition. These provisions would effectively silence federally funded researchers from communicating their findings on any politically sensitive topic. case_against: A cautious reader might note the comment focuses on personal concern and one provision rather than the entire rule, so one could ask whether it is just descriptive or issue-raising. But the explicit request to "not finalize this rule" goes beyond neutral concern.
text: I am a greatly concerned citizen of the United States who risks being severely affected by the proposed provisions. More specifically, I am concerned by Provision §200.205, which screens competitive federal education awards through a political lens rather than an educational one. This directly impacts me and my community because it limits opportunities for us to receive grants for educational development, high quality teacher training, and have a thorough curriculum that provides the best possible education. My individual district as well as the rest statewide would have far fewer resources and opportunities due to prioritizing political disputes over quality education. I strongly urge OMB to withdraw provision §200.205 and not finalize this rule. Thank you for your consideration.

evidence: "I strongly urge you to reject this proposal. Research funding should be awarded through an independent, expert peer-review process rather than political decision-making."
case_for: The comment explicitly asks OMB to "reject this proposal" and argues against shifting funding decisions from expert peer review to political decision-making. It also warns that the proposal would undermine scientific independence and evidence-based research.
case_against: A strained reading could say the commenter is mostly expressing a general principle about how research should be funded rather than discussing specific regulatory text. But the direct instruction to "reject this proposal" makes that neutral reading weak.
text: I strongly urge you to reject this proposal. Research funding should be awarded through an independent, expert peer-review process rather than political decision-making. We achieve scientific advances when funding is based on scientific merit and potential impact, not political priorities. Allowing politicians to determine which research receives funding risks undermining scientific independence, discouraging innovation, and shifting priorities away from evidence-based research toward political interests. Preserving the integrity and independence of the research funding process is CRITICAL to innovation, public trust, and the nation's future. Science must remain neutral. It is the only way to verifiable and repeatable truth in any scientific research, and protects us from junk science that might otherwise affect our health, food, medicines, ecology, environment, and technological innovations.

text: I am writing to strongly support this OMB regulation. I specifically support regulations that: Allow federal agencies to terminate active grants at any time if they are deemed inconsistent with program goals or agency priorities. [200.340] Prohibit the use of federal funds for research collaborations with foreign entities affiliated with countries under sanction by the United States, unless exceptions are authorized by federal law or the head of a federal agency. [200.220] Disallow federal grants from being used for most publication costs and open access fees. [200.461] Require that grant recipients obtain prior approval from federal agencies to use their funding to attend conferences or obtain professional memberships related to the scientific work covered by their grant. [200.432] Allow federal agencies to receive exemptions from the requirement to publicly advertise grant competitions when publicly announcing an opportunity would pose a risk to national security or is in the national interest of the United States. [200.421] Ban federal funds from being used to fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate any activities related to DEI. [200.300]

text: Thank you. I support this proposed rule because it promotes greater transparency, accountability, and responsible stewardship of federal funds while reaffirming equal treatment under the law. The proposal appropriately recognizes that faith-based organizations should be eligible to participate in federal programs on the same basis as other nonprofit organizations, provided they meet applicable program requirements. Clear, consistent standards across federal agencies will help recipients better understand their obligations while strengthening public confidence that taxpayer dollars are being used for their intended public purposes.

text: Dear OMB, I strongly support OMB's proposed rule to restore accountability to the federal grantmaking process.
